summary: Specifies how LDP can be extended to set up constraint-based routed label-switched paths, using new TLVs. This lets an operator choose paths by requirements such as bandwidth instead of only the shortest route. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Constraint-Based LSP Setup using LDP (CR-LDP) adds route and resource constraints to LDP label requests. Routers use those constraints while establishing a label-switched path through an MPLS network.

questions: how to set up constrained lsps
how does cr-ldp set up an lsp
what is an explicit route in mpls
subtitle: Extends LDP so an MPLS path can follow explicit hops and reserve resources.

tldr.problem: A path chosen only from ordinary routing information may not follow operator-selected hops or meet traffic and resource requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router sends an LDP Label Request with constraint TLVs. Routers process the requested route and resource parameters, then return a Label Mapping along the established path.
tldr.outcome: CR-LDP specifies unidirectional point-to-point constraint-based paths. RFC 3212 has been updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 7358.

today: RFC 3212 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 7358. Read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why a Path Needs Constraints
sections.content:
Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) distributes labels inside an MPLS domain. A path based only on routing tables may not satisfy traffic-engineering needs such as a particular route, bandwidth, service class or physically separate alternative paths.

CR-LDP lets an ingress Label Switching Router (LSR) initiate a path using constraints beyond ordinary routing information. This RFC defines setup for unidirectional point-to-point paths and mechanisms for reserving resources with LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary routing information may not describe every requirement for a path. CR-LDP lets the network request a path with explicit route and resource constraints.

sections.title: Route, Resource and Priority Constraints
sections.content:
An explicit route lists nodes or groups of nodes that the path must include in order. A strict hop limits the path between listed nodes; a loose hop permits other nodes between them. Group hops let the route generator describe a destination without specifying every router.

Traffic parameters describe peak and committed rates, burst sizes and service frequency. The preemption priorities rank a new path against established paths when resources are insufficient. A resource class identifies acceptable link groups, and route pinning can keep a loosely routed segment from changing its next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: An explicit route lists places the path must pass, either exactly or as a group. Other parameters describe the traffic the path must carry and how it competes for network resources.

sections.title: LDP Messages and Constraint TLVs
sections.content:
CR-LDP extends existing LDP messages with Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. The ingress sends a Label Request containing an LSP identifier and any constraints, such as an explicit route or traffic parameters. Routers forward the request downstream using ordered control; the egress sends a Label Mapping back along the path.

The specification defines TLVs for explicit routes and their hops, traffic parameters, preemption, LSP identifiers, resource classes and route pinning. If a request includes CR-LDP TLVs that a router cannot handle or satisfy, LDP notifications and status codes report the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: CR-LDP adds labeled fields to LDP's existing request and reply messages. Each field carries a kind of path instruction, such as a route hop or traffic requirement.

sections.title: How Routers Process Explicit Hops
sections.content:
Each explicit-route hop identifies an IPv4 prefix, IPv6 address, autonomous system or existing LSP. The hop's loose-or-strict bit determines whether the path may include other nodes on the way to that hop. A router that receives an unsupported hop type must stop the request and return a No Route notification.

At each router, the first hop is checked against the local node and the following hop. The router selects a next hop, removes or replaces the route information as needed, then forwards the Label Request. The exact choice among possible paths is implementation-dependent, and the router is expected to make a best effort to avoid loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router checks the next instruction in the explicit route and chooses a next hop that can reach it. It updates the route list before passing the request onward.

sections.title: Traffic Parameters and Preemption
sections.content:
The Traffic Parameters TLV carries a peak data rate, peak burst size, committed data rate, committed burst size, excess burst size, frequency and weight. Rates are expressed in bytes per second; burst sizes are in bytes. The peak data rate must be at least the committed data rate.

An LSR may lower a parameter marked negotiable. If it can support the resulting request, it reserves the resources; if not, it reports that resources are unavailable. Setup and holding priorities range from 0, the highest, to 7, the lowest. A higher-priority request may displace existing paths according to network policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The request can state traffic rates, burst sizes and how often committed service must be available. Routers reserve resources when they can, and may negotiate lower values where the request allows it.

sections.title: Setup Replies and Failure Handling
sections.content:
The Label Request travels from the ingress toward the egress. The egress returns a Label Mapping, and each intermediate router forwards that mapping to the previous router until it reaches the ingress. The mapping can carry negotiated traffic parameters so routers can adjust reservations.

If a path cannot be established, a Notification carries a status code toward the router that originated the request. When a path is preempted, routers use Withdraw and Release messages for an established LSP, or Notification and Abort messages for a request still being set up. Routers should free reserved resources when the path fails.
sections.plainLanguage: A request goes toward the destination, and a label mapping returns toward the sender. If setup fails or a path is displaced, messages report the failure and routers release its reserved resources.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: CR-LDP does not define a new security mechanism. It inherits the security mechanism specified for LDP, which protects LDP session connection streams against insertion of spoofed TCP segments.
sections.plainLanguage: CR-LDP relies on LDP's existing protection for its session connections. It does not add a separate security mechanism.
